- **What was missing at Viva Tech - and the short-cut to tech adoption Viva tech was again buzzing with innovations! AI solving for diagnostics, patient experience and overall efficiency🙌 It was all there, but still something was missing: no one talked about the human factor in adopting any of these tools🤓 It usually takes years for organizations to adopt to a totally new technology, and still not all tech innovations succeed, same with people Think of all the platforms that were creating great promises, but never got us to adopt🙄 And then there is the camera function on an iPhone. - **One of the things I enjoy most about facilitating foresight is that it asks something a little different of both the facilitator and the participants. You’re not just there to help people solve a problem or make a decision. But basically asking them to venture into uncertainty together, to suspend disbelief for a moment, to imagine alternatives, and often to let go of assumptions they actually didn’t even realise they were carrying around. Everyone arrives with their own idea of what “the future” is, and that’s part of what makes it such an interesting room to facilitate. Yesterday, Darwin and I kicked off the second cohort of 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗙𝗼𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝗙𝗮𝗰𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗼𝗿, starting with Design & Develop (photo of Darwin here doing what he does best) 💡 One thing we learned from the first cohort was that we probably tried to cover a bit too much in the opening session. It all came together in the end, but there was a fairly steep learning curve before participants got to apply everything between sessions. So this time we cut things back. Don't get me wrong, it's not because the frameworks weren’t useful, but because the story became stronger with fewer of them. Sometimes subtraction really is the better design choice. The group is fantastic already. Eight countries, five continents, people from NGOs, the public sector and private companies. It might sound like a niche topic—facilitating foresight—but people bring such different experiences that everyone ends up learning from each other! 🌹 One of my favourite parts of the first day is our final Rose, Bud, Thorn reflection. Especially the buds, the thoughts people leave with that are still forming. Yesterday they ranged from facilitation being “almost psychology” to questions about designing for Gen Z, making future personas feel grounded rather than fictional, routing insights into action, and reading a room’s readiness before you even begin. Those are exactly the conversations I was hoping we’d have. And now comes my favourite part! Over the next week-ish they’ll work in pairs to design a short futures workshop, and next session they’ll facilitate it for us and each other. That’s where theory becomes practice, and where Darwin and I probably learn just as much as the cohort does.**

- **When a foresight training ends with the client initiating an open reflection on how they want to take foresight further, and the answers are both diverse, grounded, and full of curiositym, you know something 𝘭𝘢𝘯𝘥𝘦𝘥. That exact thing happened, when I taught a strategic foresight masterclass recently for the innovation department of a pharma company. The session itself was a pilot and an introduction to the field: core concepts, mindsets, methods, and how foresight can support better strategic conversations. This team is very clear that they are not looking for a one-off inspiration session but that the goal with learning is super concrete: 𝗧𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝘄𝗮𝗻𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱 𝗮 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗴𝗲𝗿, 𝗱𝗶𝘃𝗶𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻–𝘄𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝗳𝗿𝗮𝗺𝗲𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸. A more coherent methodology, a clearer end-to-end process with stronger capabilities across the team and better bridges between signals, sensemaking, strategic options, stakeholder activation, and action. That is the dream, really! 🌟 The day had a dual purpose: introduce foresight, yes, but also use the room to understand what people actually need from foresight. And the perspectives were wonderfully wide. → Some wanted to get better at collecting signals and knowing the difference between signal and noise. → Some wanted stronger sensemaking practices. → Some were focused on how to turn insights into action. → Others were already thinking about how to activate stakeholders and make foresight usable across the organisation. That range tells me a lot. It shows not only an appetite for the work, but also a pretty mature understanding of what foresight can and cannot do. Also: I changed the plan several times during the day. I had an ambitious progression ready, but as the room moved, I moved with it. I switched the order, skipped parts, combined exercises differently, and followed what felt most useful for the learning rather than what was pre-decided on the agenda. That is always a bit risky but it is also what facilitation. You design carefully enough to know where you are going, and then you stay present enough to change the route. This was the first step in a longer collaboration, including follow-up sessions and coaching with members of their teams. There is a lot more to uncover. But the starting point is strong: serious ambition, real curiosity, and a desire to make foresight something that supports the full journey from understanding change to making better choices. A dream client, honestly.**
